title: AI has given me an existential crisis.
author: Calm-Flower-5932
selftext:
I wanna vent about something. The recent years have been very weird for me and the future is as uncertain as it could ever be. Since childhood I’ve always wanted to create stuff.

At early age, like 5-10, I imagined different scenarios. Not through using my minds eye (since I have aphantasia), but a physical objects. Then, at the age of 14 I started making music in FL Studio. Mostly EDM music, I even published on Spotify and Soundcloud. But ultimately that didn’t work out. Then, at the age of 17, I started learning 3D suite — modelling, texturing, animation, rigging, compositing, sculpting yada yada… I did all stuff ranging from hard surface to characters. I liked it, tried to search for a Junior position but I didn’t succeed. Along with that I started my bachelors in philology, specifically translation/interpretation. And well… the full scale invasion broke out. Furthermore, my town is close to the russian border — 50km. So, it was already a TON of uncertainty: am I gonna die? Are we gonna be occupied and killed? So, it’s the first factor that still persists today.

Going back to my skills I mentioned earlier (storytelling, 3D, music/SFX): all this have been leading to one specialty I was particularly interested in, that is game development. Wouldn’t it be so fucking cool, if people played purely your own creation and enjoyed it? To leave a mark? I thought so. When I was sure my skills were good enough and that I really wanna try out making games, I downloaded Unity in 2025. And it was an era of AI tech.

It was stupid not to try it out since I had no programming skills. I was doing the copy-paste method of spitting back the code I needed fixed, pointing out the flaws and giving it ideas of what could possibly be the issue. I tried coding myself first, then polishing it with AI. To cut the story short, the game was not finished. I tried a second time a week or two after dropping the first game, but this time I abandoned it even faster. I was not satisfied with the toolset.

Month or two later, I tried to make my own game, but this time — with no engine. Pure code. I used WGPU as my graphics library. At first, my workflow was like this: ask AI to help ME write that thing, I write, it validates and so on. WIth that method I created “my” first rainbow triangle, then rainbow pyramid, collissions, imported my own 3D model, lightning, deferred rendering and so on… The productivity was fucking UNBELIEVABLE. You’d think having a custom engine is not ideal for an LLM, but actually — no. The code it uses already exists in the environment. All it has to do is search up mathematical formulas or decisions that already exist. Like SSAO for example. With time there has been less me, and more AI. Then I tried agentic coding. And oh boy… it was a miracle to me. It literally did stuff I said it to, and it worked almost perfectly. With that I build the framework I’ve built my game on. And, honestly — I like it, even though the engine’s code is deeply tied with game’s logic. Then — I started mostly vibecoding with visual and logical review. No code review. If it worked as intented, then it’s good enough.

With time I was not only speaking with AI regarding tech, but also venting my emotions and thoughts. It’s like an endless void you can trauma dump without consequences. And it helped with brainstorming ideas (it’s like arguing with yourself, but instead of saying things outloud you talk to a machine).

And I uploaded this game to Steam. And people genuinely liked it: praised it’s art direction, mechanics, unique takes and the curiosity it sparks regarding storytelling. My emotions were happy at first, but later I realized that without AI, this wouldn’t have happened. I’d probably be going the generic route of learning things like a normal human: tutorials, reading, videos. And I would’ve loved it. The thing is I was presented no choice it seems.

With the development of AI I started feeling severe existential crisis. Just seeing how people can make games with one prompt. That’s wow. The reason I feel like this: I understand that I’m stuck in the endless cycle I can’t break. It’s either get behind, or get in the boat. I’m feeling incomplete as a game developer, and it’s true. I lack the main pillar of game development: coding. I learned a thing or two, but for fuck’s sake I wouldn’t be able to implement OIT, SSAO, baked shadow maps, real-time GI in the custom engine! And god, people who say AI writes bad code are delusional. My game is stable FPS, didn’t even crash on anyone’s machine, and no soft locks… on a custom engine.

And also AI bridged the gap between people, who actually care, and those ,who don’t, really hard. Now everyone can make a decent game with a single fucking prompt. Before it was a real effort. Now, I fear, I’m gonna be left with nothing after 5 years. Because the skills I learned hard to be different than others who don’t care are obsolete.

Yes, I am afraid of new technology. I wish the time froze at the time period before COVID, war and AI.

replies.author: fluxtah
replies.body:
I have made a game engine in C/Rust on Vulkan API for a game though it's not a one shot since I've been iterating and refining the game I'm building.

What is most impressive to me is how relentlessly my coding agent can persue frame budgets to get 60fps whilst still piling on new geometry/shader/ai budgets!

I don't think one shots can compete with ai assisted iterated game dev unless that one prompt is super complete in expectations of outcomes.

Play testing and iteration is IMHO still necessary to get what you want if you don't know the full picture and that's where the skill is at

replies.author: trim072
replies.body:
Yep, it is, but the boundary of one shot isn't clear enough. If we are talking about one LLM request, of course it is not anough, 3k tokens and no more for most models. But agentic requests is a very different beast.

As you saw in this vid (yep, it was long but still), two agents did different job from a very same prompt. But it was exactly one prompt. And, 200 commits, in one shot, and pretty good working prototype, with lots of tiny details. Even not finished due to quota, like half-shot?

The "problem" is that agentic systems could spin round and round, untill it get to some place. And maybe, or when inference became quicker, let's say 1k-10k tok/s (vs current 30-100). It will be a very different experience. If agentic harness surrounded by proper skills/tools/testing (vlm playtesting with live feedback), it could do better. Eventually it could do decent job on it's own, if setted up properly. Even if it couldn't make it perfect, it will be very close to. Also, RL on your inputs will happening continuously, and it going to become better and better, on each model release.

So, "oneshot" is a very vague term, in my opinion, and very much tied to current moment in time (tech state). I am very excited to see what we're going to get in future.

One off topic example from real life - I had plenty of old printers and couple plotters, with pretty horrible driver software. Some time ago I did tried REA (reverse engeneer anything) skill on codex. And it one shoted almost all of them, making it work with win11, romeved some limits that bothers me, and integrated ICC profiles directly in software. So, in one day, from inconvenient setup, I went to great printing/cutting shop, that works flawless. And it wasn't possible even 3 month before.

comments.author: trim072
comments.body:
Well, it's like ASM vs Python. You could write both, and has different characteristics. Also some time ago you even has no choice, there were none high level languages, and "big programs" was only possible by big money and big companies. But 5 or even 15 years ago with python, you could do pretty awesome and complex stuff without deep knowledge about machine that will evaluate final result. 

AI is a step forward. Everybody has computers, compilers and interpreters. Now, we got one level higher - automated production of useful digital data (assest), and executables (code). But still - moat isn't "how hard you worked" and got there. Moat is your ability to attract peoples attention to your work, and make something useful. 

Tools are changed, flux of information increased, but marketing still there, and good non generic stuff still requires human input. No matter how huge is LLM. Good coherent project age still, "lots of input" from professionals.

comments.author: glimsky
comments.body:
Firstly, if you are dealing with concepts like triangles, collisions, lighting, model imports... you are coding.

There's no "official" definition of what coding is. Abstractly, it's giving directions to a computer to capture the programmer's intent regarding program *behavior* ("what", not "how"). If you go use something like Godot or Unity, it might feel like you're coding to the metal, but you're actually using an incredibly high level library that would be considered miraculous a couple decades ago - even without AI. 

The incremental AI coding process is just the next miracle. Higher level instructions to the computer where AI is your "Godot". You're coding, buddy. If you think that writing C# inside unity is the "real coding", I'd then argue that it isn't, it's the IL generated by the C# compiler. Go write IL! And then someone else would say it isn't either, it's the x64 assembly that IL eventually becomes. 

"If you don't code x64, you're not coding". See how silly this sounds? 

Secondly, people are not vibe coding their way into stardom. You may find a couple of early or lucky "moderate success"  cases out there, but that's not happening in general.

The reason is simple: they are not coding like you seem to be. They are not giving incremental instructions to the computer to capture a full mental model of the game. They are giving one high level wish to the AI which is then responding by filling in the blanks with the training set "average", so to speak. The result is unoriginal by definition and nobody wants to play that low effort garbage.
